items.stem:
Read the following review of a film adaptation of a classic novel, from an arts website.

Three stars. The new adaptation of Jane Eyre is beautiful to look at and curiously cold to feel. Every candle-lit corridor is gorgeously framed; every gust of moorland wind arrives on cue. What is missing is Jane's voice – the furious, funny first person that makes the novel a confession rather than a costume drama. Without it, she becomes someone things happen to, rather than someone who tells us what they meant.

Analyse what is gained and lost in this adaptation.
items.answer: The reviewer argues that adaptation struggles to translate first-person narration: the film's visuals (framing, weather) replace Jane's voice, turning her from narrator into object of the camera.
items.markingKey: The reviewer argues that adaptation struggles to translate first-person narration: the film's visuals (framing, weather) replace Jane's voice, turning her from narrator into object of the camera. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: "A good adaptation must include every scene from the book." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Adaptations select, compress and reinterpret; leaving out scenes can strengthen the new work.

items.stem:
Read the following restaurant review on a food blog.

Let's start with the bread, because the bread is the best thing here, and that is not entirely a compliment. The menu promises 'a journey through the Andes'; the journey, sadly, stops at the bread basket. The ceviche was tired, the service brisk to the point of rudeness, and the bill – 58 euros for two – arrived faster than the main course. Two stars. Go for the bread. Leave before the journey.

items.answer: Extended metaphor: "'a journey through the Andes'; the journey, sadly, stops at the bread basket" – the reviewer turns the menu's own metaphor against it.

items.stem:
Read the following screenplay adaptation of the opening of a novel (an original extract written for study).

EXT. RIVERBANK – DAY
Summer. The water is flat and silent. No boats. NINA (9) sits on an upturned crate, scratching marks into the wood with a stone. Fourteen marks.
INT. FAMILY KITCHEN – DAY
Blinds half-drawn. PAPA (40s) asleep at the table, still in factory overalls. MAMA (40s) stirs a pot, watching him.
NINA (O.S.)
Fifteen?
MAMA
(sharp, not turning)
Numbers are for people with jobs.
Nina's stone stops.

How does this text show the transformation of a story from page to screen?
items.answer: The novel's first-person child narration is lost; instead the film externalises Nina's counting as marks on a crate (a visual motif) and shows Papa in factory overalls, so the audience sees the job loss rather than inferring it from a naïve voice. Mama's remark becomes direct, sharp dialogue, and "Nina's stone stops" turns the child's reaction into a silent image.
items.markingKey: The novel's first-person child narration is lost; instead the film externalises Nina's counting as marks on a crate (a visual motif) and shows Papa in factory overalls, so the audience sees the job loss rather than inferring it from a naïve voice. Mama's remark becomes direct, sharp dialogue, and "Nina's stone stops" turns the child's reaction into a silent image. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "An adaptation should be judged as a work in its own right, not as a version of its source."
items.answer: Both perspectives matter: an adaptation is a new work that gains meaning from dialogue with its source.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: each medium has its own strengths; audiences may not know the source. Arguments against: adaptations invite comparison; changes carry meaning only in relation to the source. Supported judgement: Both perspectives matter: an adaptation is a new work that gains meaning from dialogue with its source. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem:
Read the following shot list from a short film (an original extract written for study).

SHOT 1 – Extreme long shot: a lone figure crosses a frozen lake at dawn.
SHOT 2 – Low-angle medium shot: the figure (ELENA, 70s) stops; her breath clouds.
SHOT 3 – Extreme close-up: a crack spreads across the ice beneath her boot. Sound: the crack amplified; the wind drops out.
SHOT 4 – Cut to black. Silence.

Evaluate how effectively the sequence uses film language to create tension or mood.
items.answer: The extreme long shot makes Elena small and isolated in a vast landscape; the low angle gives her dignity and strength; the extreme close-up on the crack creates suspense; amplified sound and the sudden silence heighten tension; the cut to black withholds the outcome, creating an open ending.
items.markingKey: The extreme long shot makes Elena small and isolated in a vast landscape; the low angle gives her dignity and strength; the extreme close-up on the crack creates suspense; amplified sound and the sudden silence heighten tension; the cut to black withholds the outcome, creating an open ending. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following fan fiction based on Jane Austen's 'Pride and Prejudice' (an original extract written for study).

Charlotte Lucas did not love Mr Collins. She had never expected to. What she loved, she discovered in the first week at Hunsford, was the small sitting room at the back of the parsonage, where he never came because the light was poor. There she read, and wrote letters to Elizabeth, and was, for two hours each afternoon, nobody's wife.

Explain how this fan fiction reinterprets its source.
items.answer: The piece borrows Austen's characters and the detail, present in the novel, that Charlotte prefers a back room her husband avoids; it shifts focalisation from Elizabeth to Charlotte, giving a minor character inner life and reframing her pragmatic marriage as a search for private freedom.
items.markingKey: The piece borrows Austen's characters and the detail, present in the novel, that Charlotte prefers a back room her husband avoids; it shifts focalisation from Elizabeth to Charlotte, giving a minor character inner life and reframing her pragmatic marriage as a search for private freedom. Read the following poem 'Penelope' (an original poem written for study).

Penelope

Twenty years I wove and unwove,
and they called it faithfulness.
No one asked what I was making
in the hours the loom stood still –
a self, thread by thread,
that no returning king could wear.

Analyse how the text relies on and changes an earlier work.
items.answer: The poem rewrites Homer's Odyssey, in which Penelope weaves a shroud by day and unravels it by night to delay her suitors while Odysseus is away for twenty years; it gives her a voice and reinterprets the weaving as self-making rather than wifely loyalty.

Let's start with the bread, because the bread is the best thing here, and that is not entirely a compliment. The menu promises 'a journey through the Andes'; the journey, sadly, stops at the bread basket. The ceviche was tired, the service brisk to the point of rudeness, and the bill – 58 euros for two – arrived faster than the main course. Two stars. Go for the bread. Leave before the journey.

items.stem:
Read the following screenplay adaptation of the opening of a novel (an original extract written for study).

EXT. RIVERBANK – DAY
Summer. The water is flat and silent. No boats. NINA (9) sits on an upturned crate, scratching marks into the wood with a stone. Fourteen marks.
INT. FAMILY KITCHEN – DAY
Blinds half-drawn. PAPA (40s) asleep at the table, still in factory overalls. MAMA (40s) stirs a pot, watching him.
NINA (O.S.)
Fifteen?
MAMA
(sharp, not turning)
Numbers are for people with jobs.
Nina's stone stops.

Analyse how film language is used in this extract.
items.answer: Scene headings move from exterior (the silent river) to interior (the dim kitchen), linking setting and mood; the off-screen voice ("O.S.") places Nina outside the adult space; half-drawn blinds create low light and concealment.

items.stem:
Read the following poem 'Penelope' (an original poem written for study).

Penelope

Twenty years I wove and unwove,
and they called it faithfulness.
No one asked what I was making
in the hours the loom stood still –
a self, thread by thread,
that no returning king could wear.

Evaluate this text as a transformative work.
items.answer: The poem rewrites Homer's Odyssey, in which Penelope weaves a shroud by day and unravels it by night to delay her suitors while Odysseus is away for twenty years; it gives her a voice and reinterprets the weaving as self-making rather than wifely loyalty.

items.stem:
Read the following review of a film adaptation of a classic novel, from an arts website.

Three stars. The new adaptation of Jane Eyre is beautiful to look at and curiously cold to feel. Every candle-lit corridor is gorgeously framed; every gust of moorland wind arrives on cue. What is missing is Jane's voice – the furious, funny first person that makes the novel a confession rather than a costume drama. Without it, she becomes someone things happen to, rather than someone who tells us what they meant.

Note in your learner portfolio how this review evaluates the adaptation, and whether you agree.
items.answer: The reviewer argues that adaptation struggles to translate first-person narration: the film's visuals (framing, weather) replace Jane's voice, turning her from narrator into object of the camera.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "An adaptation should be judged as a work in its own right, not as a version of its source."
items.answer: Both perspectives matter: an adaptation is a new work that gains meaning from dialogue with its source.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: each medium has its own strengths; audiences may not know the source. Arguments against: adaptations invite comparison; changes carry meaning only in relation to the source. Supported judgement: Both perspectives matter: an adaptation is a new work that gains meaning from dialogue with its source.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Sound matters more than image in creating tension in film."
items.answer: They work together; tension usually comes from their combination.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: silence and amplified sound create dread; scores manipulate emotion. Arguments against: framing and editing control what is seen; images often carry key information. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Fan fiction has as much literary value as published fiction."
items.answer: Value depends on the individual work; the form itself is not inferior.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it can be inventive and critical; it democratises writing. Arguments against: quality varies widely; it depends on another author's creation.
